analysis.one_liner: Doubles the income tax exemption for dependent children under 18 to $4,000.
analysis.headline: The bill to double the child tax exemption got no cosponsors, never left the Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 102nd Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have doubled the tax exemption for each dependent child under 18, from $2,000 to $4,000, letting families with children subtract more from their taxable income and pay less tax. It also changed how inflation adjustments are rounded. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with dependent children under 18. Each child's exemption would have doubled, reducing taxable income by an extra $2,000 per child, which at tax rates of the era was worth several hundred dollars per child per year. The bill's stated findings said the exemption had eroded against inflation and, if it had kept pace, would be worth $6,000 to $7,800 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the personal exemption for a dependent child under 18 from $2,000 to $4,000, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 1991 [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state the exemption's erosion over decades had 'exacted an inordinate financial penalty on families with children' and that the full inflation-adjusted value would be roughly $6,000 to $7,800, with $4,000 as a step toward that goal [S3].
Changes the rounding of annual inflation adjustments to the nearest multiple of $10 instead of down to the next lowest $50, which slightly increases the size of yearly adjustments [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Lower exemptions mean more revenue, so doubling the child exemption would have reduced federal receipts by whatever the doubled exemption cost, made up eventually through other taxes, borrowing, or lower spending.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the exemption for every child under 18 would have reduced federal revenue, a cost the bill does not offset or pay for anywhere in its text [S3].

Exemptions reduce taxable income, so the dollar benefit is larger for families in higher tax brackets, and families with no taxable income would get nothing from it — a design that gives more help to middle- and upper-income parents than to the poorest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief for families with children was real and the bill's underlying point — the exemption had lost much of its value to inflation — was accurate by its own findings. But the design was blunt: it was unpaid-for revenue loss, and because exemptions only help people who owe income tax, it did the least for the families struggling most. A serious version would have addressed both.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Wolf introduced the bill on May 9, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury kept the revenue that doubling the child exemption would have cost. Families with young children got no tax relief, since the bill never advanced beyond its referral to committee.

for.name: Rep. Frank Wolf
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued findings arguing the child exemption had eroded against inflation and penalized families with children.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to show a partisan split; the bill was a Republican-sponsored measure with zero cosponsors of either party and never reached the floor.

industries.note: The unpaid-for exemption increase would have reduced federal receipts, a cost spread across all taxpayers. That cost is the same public that families with children draw on, so the industry interest and the public's were the same pool of money.
